title: Apalutamide: prostate cancer with ongoing ADT
context_label: High-risk nonmetastatic castration-resistant or metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer
indication_text: High-risk nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, or metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, together with ADT. Your team confirms the indication and its separate eligibility criteria.
purpose: This treatment aims to control prostate cancer and delay progression. The expected benefit depends on your disease setting, previous treatment and general health.
schedule_summary: Apalutamide 240 mg once daily, continuously while helping and tolerated, with ongoing ADT unless surgically castrated. Lower prescribed doses are 180 mg or 120 mg daily when indicated.
administration_text: Take at the same time each day, with or without food. Swallow tablets whole with water. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible that day and return to the usual schedule the next day; never take extra tablets to make up a dose. If you cannot swallow the tablet, a pharmacist must teach the correct preparation for your 60 mg or 240 mg formulation or feeding tube.
monitoring_summary: Repeat blood count, kidney and liver tests on the schedule agreed with your team. Thyroid function and ECG as clinically indicated. If warfarin is unavoidable, INR weekly until the dose is stable. The NCCP regimen does not set one fixed interval for every routine blood test.

agents.name: Apalutamide
agents.explanation: Apalutamide blocks several steps in androgen receptor signalling. In hormone-sensitive metastatic disease it can strengthen initial treatment; in selected nonmetastatic resistant disease it can delay metastases. ADT continues alongside it.
agents.watch: Report rash promptly. Blisters, peeling skin, fever with rash, or mouth/eye sores need immediate medical advice. New or worsening cough or breathlessness requires urgent assessment for lung inflammation. Seizures require emergency help. Discuss driving and medicine interactions.
risks: Rash, including rare severe blistering or systemic skin reactions
Fatigue, hot flushes, falls and fractures
Underactive thyroid, weight loss, diarrhoea and joint pain
Seizures and ischaemic heart or cerebrovascular events
Rare lung inflammation, which can be severe or fatal
Strong interactions with other medicines; sexual or fertility effects alongside ADT

anatomy: Report troublesome fatigue, falls or confusion. Seizure, collapse or sudden neurological symptoms need emergency help.
Keep thyroid blood tests. An underactive thyroid can cause fatigue, weight changes or feeling cold; report new symptoms.
Keep blood-pressure checks. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness needs urgent help; report ankle swelling or palpitations.
Keep liver blood tests. Report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced appetite or a major change in wellbeing.
New or worsening cough or breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Treatment-related lung inflammation can be severe.
Report a new rash. Severe rash with blisters, peeling, fever or mouth/eye sores needs urgent assessment.
Discuss erections, libido, fertility and contraception. Avoid exposing a pregnant partner to these medicines; follow the product-specific precautions.
Discuss bone-density assessment, falls prevention, suitable resistance and aerobic activity, calcium intake and vitamin D needs.

items.title: Why ADT continues
items.text: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) lowers testosterone from the testes. This medicine adds another form of hormone-pathway blockade. Even when cancer becomes castration-resistant, continued testosterone suppression remains part of this treatment unless you have had surgical castration.

items.title: Deciding together
items.text: This treatment aims to slow cancer growth and help control symptoms. Your team explains the expected benefit, uncertainty and alternatives for your situation.

items.title: Review and alternatives
items.text: Continue your prescribed androgen deprivation therapy (ADT), unless you have had surgery to remove both testes. The team reviews symptoms, blood tests, PSA and scans according to your own plan; there is no universal scan interval. Discuss suitable alternatives, supportive care and the option of declining treatment.

items.title: Where radiotherapy fits
items.text: Radiotherapy may treat the prostate, a recurrence or a troublesome site such as a painful bone lesion. Its purpose depends on your disease setting. Ask the team whether it belongs in your plan; starting these tablets does not itself schedule or replace radiotherapy.

evidence.title: What the evidence can tell you
evidence.intro: Research supports a treatment discussion; it cannot predict one person’s outcome.
evidence.population: High-risk nonmetastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, or metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, together with ADT. Your team confirms the indication and its separate eligibility criteria.
evidence.comparison: The exact comparison and population stated below; no comparison across trials is implied.
evidence.interpretation: TITAN’s 2019 metastatic hormone-sensitive analysis reported 24-month overall survival of 82.4% with apalutamide plus ADT versus 73.5% with placebo plus ADT (HR 0.67; 95% CI 0.51–0.89). SPARTAN in high-risk nonmetastatic resistant disease reported median time to metastasis or death of 40.5 versus 16.2 months (HR 0.28; 95% CI 0.23–0.35). These are different populations and endpoints; time without metastasis is not the same as lifespan.
limitations: Trial populations and schedules differ; comparisons across separate trials are unreliable.
An improvement in progression-free survival is not automatically an overall-survival benefit.
